What this ad blocker test checks

Three independent checks, scored together. No real ads or trackers are ever loaded.

Cosmetic filters

Two ad-shaped elements, one static and one added after load. The test measures whether your blocker removes or hides them.

Ad script loading

Two decoy scripts named ads.js and pagead.js. The test measures whether they were stopped from running.

Host and DNS blocking

128 hostnames across 30 ad, analytics, tracking and telemetry services. This is the only category a DNS filter can score on.

Testing a DNS filter: Pi-hole, AdGuard Home, NextDNS, AdGuard DNS or Control D

A DNS filter blocks domains, so it can only pass the Host category. Here is the score to expect and how to read it.

What a good Pi-hole score looks like

A DNS filter on its own answers 128 of the 132 checks, so roughly 40–60% is the correct result, not a failure. The four cosmetic and script checks need a browser extension, which no DNS resolver can do. If you want to know whether your Pi-hole is working, look at the Host category, not the total.

Turn the block page off first

Pi-hole, AdGuard Home and NextDNS can answer a blocked domain with their own block page instead of dropping the request. To this test that looks like a successful connection, so your score drops even though the domain was blocked. Set the blocking mode to NXDOMAIN or NULL and re-run.

Getting to a full score

Pair the DNS filter with a browser extension such as uBlock Origin or the AdGuard extension. The DNS layer covers the hosts, the extension covers the cosmetic filters and the ad scripts. That combination is what scores green here.

Written Pi-hole, pi-hole or pihole — all the same thing, and the same advice applies to AdGuard Home, AdGuard DNS, Control D, Quad9 and any other resolver-level blocker. The test cannot see per-client rules, regex filters or allowlists — only whether the 128 hostnames above resolved.

Answers about how the test works, what your score means, and how to improve it.
